REVIEW: Prime Video’s ‘Drawn Together’ is Powered by Chemistry
  • Diya Gohil
  • September 8, 2026
  • 8:48 PM
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:18
Instaread

There are some romances where you spend half the film waiting to feel the spark everyone on screen keeps insisting is there. Drawn Together certainly doesn’t have that problem. From the moment Marfil (Ester Expósito) and Sebastian (Hugo Diego García) are thrown together, there is a buzz between them that becomes almost impossible to look away from.

Adapted from Marfil, the first novel in Mercedes Ron’s bestselling Enfrentados duology, Drawn Together follows Marfil Cortés (Expósito), the fiercely independent daughter of a Spanish business tycoon. After Marfil is mysteriously kidnapped in New York and subsequently released, her father takes no chances with her safety, assigning the guarded Sebastián Moore (García) as her personal bodyguard. Unsurprisingly, neither is particularly thrilled about the arrangement.

What follows isn’t necessarily unfamiliar territory. Forced proximity, clashing personalities and a bodyguard who takes his job extremely seriously provide all the ingredients for exactly the kind of romance you expect. Drawn Together isn’t particularly interested in reinventing that formula either. Instead, it leans wholeheartedly into it.

And that’s largely why it works.

Expósito and García are unbelievable together. The tension between Marfil and Sebastián is easily the film’s biggest strength, building through lingering looks, arguments and those moments where neither character really needs to say what they’re thinking. There is a genuine electricity whenever they’re sharing the screen, and director Óscar Pedraza clearly understands exactly how long to let that tension linger.

Expósito is particularly good at capturing the contradictions within Marfil. She is strong-willed, rebellious and deeply resistant to having her freedom taken away, but there is also fear underneath that confidence. After everything she has experienced, her determination to remain in control feels as much like self-preservation as defiance. Expósito allows that vulnerability to emerge without ever diminishing the strength that defines her.

García proves an equally compelling match. Sebastián could easily have fallen into the familiar mould of the mysterious, brooding bodyguard, but there is enough warmth beneath his guarded exterior to make him more interesting. His protectiveness towards Marfil gradually reveals another side to him, and García handles that shift without losing the mystery surrounding the character.

Together, they give Drawn Together more depth than its relatively conventional romantic foundations might suggest.

The film also benefits from the mystery running alongside the central relationship. Marfil’s kidnapping leaves questions hanging over the story, allowing Pedraza to occasionally pull the film towards thriller territory. It doesn’t always balance those elements perfectly, and there are points where the plot surrounding the romance feels less compelling than Marfil and Sebastián themselves.

There is also an unavoidable familiarity to much of it. Anyone well-versed in this particular corner of romantic fiction will recognise several of its beats long before they arrive. But when the chemistry is this convincing, predictability isn’t necessarily fatal.

Sometimes you simply want the tension, the longing and two people who clearly shouldn’t be looking at each other like that. Drawn Together delivers all three.

Drawn Together may not completely escape the conventions of the genre, but Expósito and García make it incredibly easy to get swept up in Marfil and Sebastián’s story. And with a cliffhanger that makes it abundantly clear their story is far from finished, Prime Video knows exactly how to leave romance fans wanting the already-confirmed sequel. 

Drawn Together

September 9, 2026
Network/Studio:

Óscar Pedraza
